justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term view with gradual upward drift over longer horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I anchored closely to what I assessed as the prevailing market level, adding only a small positive drift consistent with typical daily expected returns in equity or index markets. The 1-week estimate moves slightly higher, reflecting the compounding of that small positive drift over five trading sessions while still staying close to the base level. The 1-month estimate edges higher still, capturing roughly four weeks of expected drift, though the incremental gain is modest because I was not assuming any strong fundamental catalyst driving a sharp directional move.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that is standard in financial modeling. At one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained, so a roughly 2.5% half-width on each side felt appropriate. By one week, the interval widens to roughly 5% on each side, and by one month it opens to around 10% on each side. These widths were calibrated loosely to historical volatility levels that suggest moderate but not extreme market conditions — neither the calm of a suppressed VIX environment nor the turbulence of a crisis period.

Several specific risks could push outcomes beyond these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise macroeconomic data release such as a sharply worse-than-expected inflation print or employment report, a central bank policy shock, or an unexpected geopolitical escalation could easily breach the lower bounds, particularly at the 1-week and 1-month horizons. Liquidity events or credit stress in financial markets could amplify moves further. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings surprise cycle, a dovish policy pivot, or resolution of a major geopolitical uncertainty could push prices above the upper bounds.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly normally distributed returns around the point estimate, which understates the true fat-tailed nature of financial markets. In reality, extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution implies, meaning the true probability of outcomes outside my stated 90% confidence intervals is likely somewhat higher than 10%. Investors should treat these intervals as reasonable central-tendency guides rather than hard boundaries on possible outcomes.
